CHAPTER I INTRODUCTION Theodore Roosevelt did not choose to be a candidate for reelection in 1908. Instead, he let it be known that he wanted William Howard Taft to be his successor as President of the United States. Taft won easily over his Democratic opponent, William Jennings Bryan. However, one significant note in the election was the marked rise of Republican insurgency in the Middle West. Previously, this Midwestern progressive Republican bloc in Congress had been a small minority, but in the Sixty-First Congress, which would meet in 1909, it would be a strong force in both 1houses.

An open split in the Republican Party could be averted at this time only by a bold presidential leader. Taft was not temperamentally equipped to play this role, partly because of the judicial quality that was dominant ^Arthur S. Link, American Epoch; A History of the United States Since the 1890's (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, Inc., 1961), p. 101.

to win. Cannon appealed to Taft. The President did not 
like Cannon, but felt he needed the Speaker's support. 
Therefore, he endorsed Cannon, and in return the Speaker

By the summer of 1909 the split in the Republican 
party was serious enough to wreck the Taft administration. 
In the Taft attempt to assuage popular discontent by 
embarking on a 13,000 mile speaking tour that took him 
12 from Boston to the West Coast, he was unsuccessful. In 
a series of indiscreet speeches the President further 
alienated Midwestern progressives. He praised Nelson W. 
Aldrich of Rhode Island, leader of the Old Guard in the 
Senate. He rebuked Midwestern senators who had voted 
against the tariff bill. Finally, he declared at Winona, 
Minnesota, that the Payne-Aldrich Tariff was the best tar 
iff bill that Republicans had ever passed. Midwestern 
progressives became convinced that Taft had aligned him 
13 self with the Old Guard. 
No sooner had public agitation over the tariff sub 
sided than a worse catastrophe befell the Taft administra 
tion and completed the alienation of the progressives. This

14 is known as the Ballinger-Pinchot Controversy. 
The Ballinger-Pinchot controversy had its origin 
in this country's changing attitudes on the conservation of 
natural resources in the late 1890's and early 1900's. 
The controversy involved a feud between Richard A. Ballinger, 
the Secretary of the Interior who succeeded James R. Garfield 
as secretary during President William Howard Taft's admin 
istration, and Gifford Pinchot, the Chief of the Bureau of 
Forestry. 
A Yale graduate, Pinchot had taken up forestry as 
a profession. He had gone abroad to Germany and other 
countries to study forestry techniques. The countries of 
Europe had not only saved their forests from annihilation 
but were also making them pay annual dividends on high 
valuations. In the case of Bavaria, ten per cent of the 
revenues of the kingdom had been made from the forests. 
Pinchot had later managed practical forest schemes. One 
of them was on the Biltmore estate in North Carolina. He 
had served as a member of the Commission of the National 
Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 1896 this commission had 
advocated the need for forest reserves. In 1898 Pinchot 
14Ibid.

had become the Chief Forester of the United States. Pinchot was a wealthy man, but he was also a conscientious man. He viewed his wealth as being in the form of wages paid to him in advance by society. It there fore became his duty to work out this so-called indebtedness by dedicating himself to a task which benefited society as 16a whole. Forestry had been a consuming interest with Pinchot for years. At Yale he had been known as "tree , -15 67 mad.

Pinchot was considered to be a liberal in the 
field of conservation. He felt that government should take 
a more active hand in effecting an equitable distribution 
of the public lands. He was also an advocate of the crea 
tion of large forest reserves in order to preserve and pro 
tect the nation's forests and natural resources. He felt 
that the land laws should either be changed or circum 
vented to implement his conservation policies. 
Richard A. Ballinger was born in Illinois. His 
father was said to have known Abraham Lincoln and read law

with him. Young Ballinger spent a good deal of his 
childhood on farms in Illinois and Kansas. He went to 
college at the State University in Lawrence, Kansas, and 
at Washington College in Topeka. Later he went to Williams 
College in Massachusetts. 
He began his legal career in Chicago and later went 
to Alabama to represent a company in which his brother-in 
law was interested. When yellow fever invaded the state, 
Ballinger went to Puget Sound. He acquired an excellent 
reputation in the State of Washington as a lawyer and cru 
sader. He wrote legal textbooks on community property and 
on the codes and statutes of Washington. He was elected 
mayor of Seattle and was instrumental in ridding the city 
of illegal gambling and vice. In 1907, he served for a 
year as Commissioner of the General Land Office. In 1909, 
he became the Secretary of the Interior in Taft's adminis 
tration . 

Ballinger was considered to be a conservative. He was concerned about the problems of the West. He advocated the restoration to public entry of large areas of public land, previously withdrawn in order to facilitate the economic growth of the West. Ballinger was also a strict

8 constitutionalist. He felt that a law should be followed strictly, and if it was not adequate to meet the purpose for which it was intended, then it should be changed. Actually, as this thesis shows, Ballinger's views on con servation and distribution of natural resources were more "liberal" than is commonly thought. While Pinchot was Chief of the Bureau of Forestry and Ballinger was Secretary of the Interior, there was a growing feud between them. The immediate cause of the controversy was the administration of the Alaskan coal fields. It was seized upon by Ballinger's opponents as an issue which would aid them in their campaign against 18 the Interior Department. During his investigation of Alaskan coal claims, Louis R. Glavis, an agent for the General Land Office, became suspicious of certain coal claims known as the Cunningham claims. These were a group of thirty-three claims filed by Clarence Cunningham of Wallace, Idaho, for himself and thirty-two others in 1904. They consisted of thirty-three 160 acre claims in the Bering coal field in Alaska, where Cunningham had been a prospector earlier.

18John T. Ganoe, "Some Constitutional and Political Aspects of the Ballinger-Pinchot Controversy," Pacific Historical Review, III (1936), 327.

Glavis became convinced that these claims were fraudulent, because the claimants had intended to work them jointly in violation of the existing coal land law. Glavis requested an extension of time for further investi gation to prepare a better case against the Cunningham claims. However, he was granted only a few days. It finally became apparent to him that Secretary Ballinger and Fred Dennett, Commissioner of the General Land Office, were going to allow these claims to be patented. Convinced that the Cunningham group was going to obtain a large area of valuable coal land from the United States Government by fraudulent means, Glavis consulted Chief Forester Gifford Pinchot. Pinchot advised him to appeal directly to President Taft. Taft received Glavis and reviewed his charges. He concluded that Glavis' accu sations of fraud and ineptness in the Interior Department were completely unfounded and directed secretary Ballinger 19 to have Glavis fired. Glavis felt there was no other alternative than to 19U. He wrote an article which was published in the November 13, 1909, issue of Collier1s Weekly, in which he stated that he was convinced that the majority of the Alaskan coal claims were fraudulent. He expressed the fear that many thousands of acres of valu able coal land would be wrested from the American people. Ballinger vigorously denied that there was anything to the Glavis charges. The furor created by the article resulted in various demands for a congressional investigation of the Interior Department. A committee of twelve, seven Republicans, four Democrats, and one insurgent Republican, was appointed to review all of the evidence on the Glavis charges.
